title: durationStartDate / durationEndDate are parsed with a hardcoded DD/MM/YYYY, ignoring the arguments

oracle.activityBoundary: every callActivity argument and return value crosses oracle/lib/boundary.js
oracle.determinismCheck: the case was run twice at clockPinIso and the two document arrays compared

edits: hearing: prosecutionCases[0].defendants[0].offences[0].judicialResults replaced with the real fixture judicialResult-with-durationElement.json (fixtures/judicial-results/, copied byte-identically from the function app's Mapper/test tree).

that grafted result: durationElement.durationStartDate set to "03/04/2019" and durationElement.durationEndDate to "2021-07-26" — one DD/MM/YYYY value and one ISO value, so the single hardcoded parse is visible on both.

that grafted result: isAvailableForCourtExtract true, publishedForNows false, orderedDate "2020-01-20" — the minimum needed for the court-extract filter (RegisterFragmentService.js:6) to keep it and for the date sort to behave as in the base case.

digests.convention: sha256 of the written file bytes — `sha256sum <file>` reproduces each value exactly

nodeEvidence.what: `dateService.formatDateAndGetLocalDateTime(durationElement.durationStartDate)` — called with ONE argument, so sourceFormat and targetFormat are undefined.
formatDateAndGetLocalDateTime(dateString, sourceFormat, targetFormat) forwards all three to formatDate...
...and formatDate IGNORES sourceFormat and targetFormat entirely: `return moment(dateString, 'DD/MM/YYYY').format('YYYY-MM-DD');`. The parameters exist only to make the call sites look configurable.

assertion: The hearing's offence results are replaced with the real judicialResult-with-durationElement.json fixture — whose own dates are "26/02/2019" and "26/07/2021", i.e. the producer really does send DD/MM/YYYY — and the two dates are then changed to expose the parse: durationStartDate "03/04/2019" (DD/MM/YYYY) and durationEndDate "2021-07-26" (ISO). Assert EXACTLY, on the TFL document's single offence result, resultData: (1) durationStartDate is the STRING "2019-04-03T00:00:00Z" — the DD/MM/YYYY input read as 3 April, correctly for this producer; (2) durationEndDate is the STRING "Invalid dateZ" — the ISO input is NOT understood, moment returns the literal "Invalid date", and DateService.js:42 appends "Z" and POSTs it into a field the frozen contract types as a date-time; (3) durationValue is the STRING "5" and secondaryDurationValue the STRING "2", not numbers (ResultDataMapper.js:21,23 call .toString()); (4) durationUnit "M", secondaryDurationUnit "Y". Assertion (2) is the one that matters. It shows the hardcoded parse is not a harmless mislabel — a date arriving in any format other than DD/MM/YYYY is silently converted into a garbage string and shipped. A java.time port using ISO_LOCAL_DATE, or a lenient multi-format parser that gets both dates right, disagrees with this recording on both fields and MUST fail. D11 is priority-3 but the same rule applies: correcting the parse changes values prosecuting authorities read, so it ships with a DEVIATIONS.md entry or it does not ship. See also s05-invalid-date-z-shipped-as-a-timestamp — the same "Invalid dateZ" leak, reached from a different direction on an unmodified fixture.
